The figure above shows the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ and its inverse $y=f^{-1}(x).$ The point $A$ has coordinates $(2, 0)$ and lies on $y=f(x).$
The point $B$ has coordinates $(0,2)$ and lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$ If $f'(2)=-\dfrac{3}{2},$ what is $(f^{-1})'(0)?$
e-14720.worked_solution:
Since $B \,(0,2)$ lies on $f^{-1},$ we have $f^{-1}(0) = 2.$ We're also told that $f'(2)=-\dfrac{3}{2}.$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse function is

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

e-14719.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function
e-14719.problem: Consider the function $f(x) = \dfrac{2-3x}{4+5x}$ and the point $P\left(-1,-5\right)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y=f^{-1}(x)$ at the point $\left(-5,-1\right).$
e-14719.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(-1, -5).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2-3x}{4+5x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{22}{(4+5x)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =-22\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(-1, -5)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(-5, -1)$ lies on $y=f^{-1}(x).$ 

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(-5) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(-5))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-22)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{22}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

e-14721.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function Using a Table
e-14721.problem:
The following table gives the values of $f(x), f'(x),g(x),$ and $g'(x)$ at some points. Find $(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(1)$ of the product of functions.

| **$x$** | $f(x)$ | $f'(x)$ | $g(x)$ | $g'(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $-3$ | $1$ |
| $2$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $3$ | $5$ |
e-14721.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse $f^{-1}(x)$ is

$$
(f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function $f^{-1}(x)g(x)$ is

$$
(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(x)=\dfrac{g(x)}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}+g'(x)f^{-1}(x).
$$

Substituting $x=1,$ we have

$$
(f^{-1}\cdot g)'(1) =\dfrac{g(1)}{f'(f^{-1}(1))}+g'(1)f^{-1}(1).
$$

From the table, we obtain $f^{-1}(1)=2,$ $g(1)=-3,$ $g'(1)=1,$ and $f'(2)=-1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1}\cdot g)^{′}(1) & =\frac{g(1)}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))}+{g}^{′}(1){f}^{-1}(1) \\  & =\frac{-3}{{f}^{′}(2)}+1\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{-3}{-1}+2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

e-14722.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
e-14722.problem: Consider the function $f(x) =3e^{x}-1.$ Given that $y = f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $(f^{-1})'(2).$
e-14722.worked_solution:
To determine $(f^{-1})'(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
\left(f^{-1}\right)'(2) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of $f^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation $f^{-1}(2) = x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ 3{e}^{x}-1 & =2 \\ 3{e}^{x} & =3 \\ {e}^{x} & =1 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f^{-1}(2) = 0.$

Now, we calculate $f'(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3{e}^{x}-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{e}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3{e}^{0} \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3+4x}{2-3x}$ and the point $P(1,-7)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(-7,1).$
after.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(1,-7).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3+4x}{2-3x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{17}{(2-3x)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(1) & =17\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(1,-7)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(-7,1)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(-7) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(-7))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{17}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(7,\frac{3}{4}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3}{2\sqrt{x-3}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{3}{4(x-3)^{3/2}} \\ {f}^{′}(7) & =-\frac{3}{32}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(7,\frac{3}{4})$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(\frac{3}{4},7)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(\frac{3}{4}) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(\frac{3}{4}))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(7)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{3}{32})} \\  & =-\frac{32}{3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

content.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{x-3}}$ and the point $P(7,\frac{3}{4})$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(\frac{3}{4},7).$
content.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(7,\frac{3}{4}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3}{2\sqrt{x-3}} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{3}{4(x-3)^{3/2}} \\ {f}^{′}(7) & =-\frac{3}{32}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(7,\frac{3}{4})$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(\frac{3}{4},7)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(\frac{3}{4}) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(\frac{3}{4}))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(7)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{3}{32})} \\  & =-\frac{32}{3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

The formula for the derivative of the inverse f−1(x) is (f−1)′(x)=1f′(f−1(x)).

Using this, and the product rule, the derivative of the function f−1(x)g(x) is (f−1⋅g)′(x)=g(x)f′(f−1(x))+g′(x)f−1(x).

Substituting x=4, we have (f−1⋅g)′(4)=g(4)f′(f−1(4))+g′(4)f−1(4).

From the table, we obtain f−1(4)=3, g(4)=−1, g′(4)=5, and f′(3)=−2. Therefore,

(f−1⋅g)′(4)=g(4)f′(f−1(4))+g′(4)f−1(4)=−1f′(3)+5⋅3=−1−2+15=312.

after.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
({g}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{g}^{′}({g}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=2,$ we have

$$
({g}^{-1})^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{g}^{′}({g}^{-1}(2))}.
$$

From the table, we obtain ${g}^{-1}(2)=5$ and ${g}^{′}(5)=-5.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({g}^{-1})^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{g}^{′}({g}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{g}^{′}(5)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-5)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(3) & =x \\ f(x) & =3 \\ \sqrt{2x-1} & =3 \\ 2x-1 & =9 \\ 2x & =10 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}

$$

content.problem: Consider the function $f(x)={x}^{3}+5x+2.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$
content.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ {x}^{3}+5x+2 & =2 \\ x({x}^{2}+5) & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=0.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{3}+5x+2 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}+5 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =3\cdot 0+5 \\ {f}^{′}(0) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
